title: Communities and Roles
subject: Social Studies
developmentNotes: Grade 3 students understand concrete community roles but need support connecting roles, needs, responsibilities, and cooperation.
learningObjective: Students will identify community roles, explain how roles help meet community needs, and support claims with examples.
essentialQuestion: How do different people help a community work?

vocabularyTerms.definition: a group of people who live, work, or learn together
a job or responsibility someone has
something people must have to live or be safe

prerequisites: Know examples of local places and workers
Understand basic needs like food, safety, and learning

hook.content: Students see a community map with a school, fire station, library, clinic, grocery store, and park. They choose one place and explain who helps there.
hook.studentAction: Predict, notice, or explain initial thinking before direct instruction.
hook.teacherOrAppAction: Capture initial response as non-graded diagnostic evidence.

learningGoal.content: I can students will identify community roles, explain how roles help meet community needs, and support claims with examples.
successCriteria: I can explain the core concept in my own words.
I can show evidence or reasoning, not only an answer.
I can correct a common mistake.

miniTeach.content: A community works because people have roles. Roles help meet needs. Teachers help people learn. Firefighters help with safety. Librarians help people find information. Community members also have responsibilities, like following rules and caring for shared spaces.
miniTeach.cognitiveLoadNotes: Use short chunks, one example at a time, and reveal labels only after students observe the model.

firstPrinciplesBreakdown.coreConcept: Communities are systems of people, places, needs, and responsibilities.
known: People in a community need safety, learning, food, health, and shared spaces.
unknown: Which role best meets a specific need.
rules: A role should connect to a need or service.
Communities work better when people cooperate.
Citizens have responsibilities even if they do not have a paid job.
avoid: Do not assume only paid workers help a community.
Do not confuse a place with a role.
Do not ignore responsibilities of ordinary community members.
steps: Identify who or what helps meet that need.
Describe how cooperation helps the whole community.
firstPrinciplesBreakdown.check: If removing a role causes a community need to go unmet, that role is important.

workedExample.content: Need: people need to learn. Role: teacher. Evidence: teachers explain lessons, answer questions, and help students practice. Reasoning: this helps the community because educated people can solve problems and help others.
workedExample.teacherOrAppAction: Highlight each reasoning step and connect it to the first-principles breakdown.

items: Match community needs to roles: safety/firefighter, learning/teacher, health/nurse.
Sort cards into place, role, and responsibility.
Explain how a library helps a community.
Discuss one responsibility students have in a classroom community.
guidedPractice.scaffolding: Start with high support, then remove hints. Require explanation on the final item.

criticalThinkingCheckpoint.prompt: A student says only firefighters and doctors help communities. What is missing from this thinking?
criticalThinkingCheckpoint.lookFor: Student identifies assumption, evaluates reasoning, and explains why one answer or model is stronger.

evidenceBasedReasoningTask.prompt: Claim: A library helps a community. Use two examples as evidence and explain why they matter.

interpretationOrDiscussionTask.prompt: Interpret the community map: Which places are connected to safety, learning, health, and recreation?
interpretationOrDiscussionTask.safety: Use private response or moderated classroom mode only. No unrestricted student chat.

activePractice.content: Students build a mini community map and place role cards where they meet needs. The app asks them to explain one connection.

reteachPath.misconception: Student confuses places with roles or thinks only paid workers help communities.
reteachPath.simpleExplanation: A place is where something happens. A role is what someone does to help.
steps: Separate place cards from role cards.

practice.answer: Library is a place; librarian is a role.

reteachPath.exitCriteria: Student completes at least 4 of 5 reteach items and explains the corrected misconception.

tasks: Design a community map that includes at least six roles and explain how each meets a need.
Choose a community problem and propose a solution using three roles.
Compare a classroom community to a town community.
challengePath.extensionRule: Unlock at 90+ mastery or teacher/parent assignment; still schedule Memory Vault review.

successCriteria: I can identify a community need.
I can explain how roles help a community.
I can suggest a fair solution.

knowledge: Communities use shared roles and decisions to meet needs.
capability: Describe a role and its responsibility.
reasoning: Compare how choices affect people in a community.
retention: Recall the role-need-responsibility connection after a delay.
transfer: Apply the idea to a new classroom, neighborhood, or online community.

phaseModules.title: Notice a community need
phaseModules.studentAction: Identify one need people must solve together.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can name the need and my clue.

phaseModules.title: See roles in action
phaseModules.studentAction: Follow a model showing how roles cooperate to meet a need.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can connect a role to a responsibility.

phaseModules.title: Sort needs and roles
phaseModules.studentAction: Sort cards into need, role, responsibility, rule, and result.

phaseModules.title: Build a community map
phaseModules.studentAction: Connect roles to actions that meet a shared need.

phaseModules.title: Compare choices
phaseModules.studentAction: Compare two solutions and explain who is helped or left out.
phaseModules.successCheck: I use fairness and evidence language.

phaseModules.title: Propose a solution
phaseModules.studentAction: Solve a new community scenario with roles and responsibilities.
phaseModules.successCheck: My proposal is supported by reasons.

phaseModules.title: Retrieve the role loop
phaseModules.studentAction: Recall need, role, responsibility, action, and result after a delay.

phaseModules.title: Use the loop elsewhere
phaseModules.studentAction: Apply the reasoning to a classroom or neighborhood problem.

phaseModules.title: Repair or extend
phaseModules.studentAction: Add a missing voice or explain how a rule could improve fairness.
phaseModules.successCheck: My next move responds to the scenario.

proofTasks.prompt: Explain how a role helps meet a community need.
Propose a solution to a new community scenario.
Retrieve the role-responsibility loop after a delay.
Apply the reasoning to a new community.

feedbackRules.result: The learner names a role but not its responsibility.
feedbackRules.hint: Ask what the person does and which need it helps meet.

feedbackRules.result: The solution ignores who is affected.
feedbackRules.hint: Name another person or group who should be heard.

reteachPaths.trigger: The learner cannot connect roles to needs.
reteachPaths.action: Use one classroom need and match three role cards to actions.

prerequisiteRepairPaths.trigger: The learner cannot identify a shared need.
prerequisiteRepairPaths.action: Sort familiar classroom routines into wants, needs, and responsibilities.

challengePaths.trigger: The learner explains a solution with multiple roles.
challengePaths.action: Revise the solution so an overlooked group has a voice.

parentTeacherNotes: When visiting a store, park, school, or library, ask: “Who helps here? What need do they help meet?”
accessibilityNotes: Use plain, grade-appropriate language and define academic vocabulary before using it in prompts.
Provide alt text or text-equivalent descriptions for every image, diagram, array, chart, map, or model.
Make all interactive elements keyboard accessible with visible focus states and screen-reader labels.
Never rely only on color to communicate correct/incorrect, categories, or importance.
Provide read-aloud support for Foundation Academy and optional read-aloud for all grade bands.
Chunk instructions into short steps and provide examples before independent work.
safetyNotes: No public student posting, random direct messages, or unrestricted discussion.
Discussion prompts must use sentence frames and moderation/teacher controls when implemented.
Student-generated work should be visible only to the student and authorized parent/teacher roles unless explicitly assigned in a safe classroom workflow.
Do not collect unnecessary personal information in lesson responses.
implementationNotes: Render lessonFlow sections in order with progress state.
Persist quiz attempts and item-level skill tags.
Generate Memory Vault records after lesson completion.
Use mastery bands to branch to reteach, guided practice, review, or challenge.
Store open responses privately with role-based access.
Use answer keys and rubrics for review; do not expose hidden answer keys in student mode.
